Tier 3 retention is the second priority: 17 of 34 Tier 3 stores slid back to Tier 2, and with the highest defaulting volume of the group (31), stabilizing the net +32 Tier 2 expansion is essential to protect the -41.9% Tier 1 reduction achieved this period.
Tim King:
PAST: Tim King's zone opened at the highest starting average of the group (3.07), absorbed a February dip to 2.98, and closed August at 3.23 (+0.16) with a sustained 3.15-3.23 band through June-August. Tier movement was heavily Tier 3-led: Tier 3 grew from 29 to 47 stores (+62.1%, the largest T3 expansion of the group) while Tier 1 fell from 53 to 41 (-22.6%), on 51 moves up versus 25 down. Tim's binding profile differs from peers: Speed overtakes Win Score as the primary Tier 2 constraint (37.6% vs 29.9%), while Win Score still leads Tier 1 (60.5% vs 23.3%).

PRESENT: The zone closes at 3.23 overall - the highest of the three OAs - across 43 Tier 1 (avg 1.90), 117 Tier 2 (avg 3.27) and 47 Tier 3 (avg 4.34) stores, with Tier 1 concentration at 20.8%. Risk posture is the strongest of the trio: 0 at-risk stores, 28 defaulting and just 14 Tier 1 watch stores, the smallest watch load among the OAs. The primary binding constraint is now Speed in Tier 2 (37.6% share). Hotspots concentrate in THAYER, LINDSEY (6 Tier 1 stores, 86% rate, area avg 2.10), Abdou, Michelle (4, 67%) and BROWN, ASHLEY (4, 57%, avg 2.18), with Culp, Brianna the zone's lowest-performing area at 1.93.

FUTURE: The single highest-impact action is a Speed improvement program across Tier 2 opening at THAYER, LINDSEY - the largest hotspot (6 Tier 1 stores, 86% rate, 2.10 average) bridging the Speed-binding issue into Tier 1 - supported by targeted work in Culp, Brianna (1.93) as the zone's weakest territory. With only 14 Tier 1 watch stores and no at-risk stores, Tim can redirect capacity toward defending the 47-store Tier 3 base (up 62.1%), where 12 of the original 29 slid back; locking in those gains while resolving the Speed bind protects the zone's current leadership position.

Performance is uniformly weak: 10 stores defaulting (22.2%) and another 7 on the T1 watch list, leaving nearly 38% of the store base in a defaulting or at-watch state. This segment is a data-ownership and governance gap as much as a performance problem — 45 stores operating without a designated FOP owner and director.

The default rate of 22.2% is by far the highest of any FOP and, absent an assigned operator, has no active management owner, meaning the risk is likely under-monitored and uncaptured in escalation loops. From there, apply the same remediation standard used for acute operators elsewhere (store-level review and payment plan) given the disproportionate 22.2% default rate, and conduct a verification pass on the FOP assignment data to ensure no additional unassigned stores exist.

_leadership_summary: The national portfolio moved from a 3.19 in January to 3.35 in August, a steady climb driven almost entirely by Tier 3 gains. Tier 3 grew from 845 stores to 1,136 — a third of the fleet now sits there — while Tier 1 contracted from 1,009 to 776. This wasn't a rising-tide story: the median store improved, but the top end thinned out. Win Score carries Tier 1 at 66.4% of its binding constraint, and that held relatively firm; the real action was in Tier 3, where Speed and Brand are co-dominant constraints at 32% each, meaning the lower tier is being pulled in two directions simultaneously and can't break out without solving both. Danielle Hudson's zone is the most striking example — she moved a quarter of her stores into Tier 3 (76.9% increase) while cutting her Tier 1 base by over a third, yet her average still climbed 0.30, the largest delta among all OAs. That's a zone converting floor stores into mid-tier performers at scale, which is exactly the portfolio play. Dustin Patton and Michael Grant posted similar T1-to-T3 conversion patterns with 40-50% Tier 1 reductions and strong average gains. On the other end, Cellesha Steel's Tier 1 actually grew 3.2% while her Tier 3 ballooned 75% — a sign of polarization that bears watching, and Jesse White barely moved the needle with a 0.01 delta across 358 stores despite the second-largest Tier 1 count in the fleet. At the franchisee level, the gap is stark: Al Salas and Mark Peterson are both above 4.0 across 49 and 68 stores respectively, while Asad Adam Mitha sits at 1.71 across 7 units — all under Betty Olvera's directorship, which suggests the issue is operational execution at the FOP level, not structural. The 309 defaulting stores and 387 Tier 1 watchlist stores represent roughly 15% of the fleet that is actively deteriorating or on the edge, and the 0.11 correlation between 5-Star and same-store sales growth tells us the business case is real but modest — improving 5-Star is necessary but won't alone drive the top line. The single national priority is clear: accelerate Tier 3 store conversion by attacking the Speed-Brand dual constraint. Speed ticked up to 2.98 in August after trending down all year, which is a warning sign that operational execution is slipping just as volume seasonality should be helping. Every OA with a Tier 3 increase above 40% needs a store-by-store action plan focused on menu accuracy and make-line discipline — those are the two controllable levers that move both Speed and Brand simultaneously. Sarah Heitz's zone, with a 0.25 delta and 42.5% Tier 3 growth, is the model to replicate; Hellen Lobaccaro's near-flat Tier 1 change (-1.5%) against 47.6% Tier 3 growth suggests stores are stalling at the bottom of Tier 2 rather than converting upward, and she needs targeted intervention. The portfolio is moving in the right direction, but the speed of movement is slowing and the tail is getting longer — the next 90 days should be about converting the T2-to-T3 pipeline into T2, not just celebrating the T1 exits.

bootcamp.narrative:
Boot Camp Leadership Narrative – September Run
August was a high-volume month: 60 workshops across 448 stores. Dustin Patton led the charge with 10 workshops and 80 stores coached, followed by Derron Spencer (7 ws / 76 stores) and Jiselle Medina (5 ws / 46 stores). YTD we've delivered 103 workshops reaching 832 stores—real momentum.
Effectiveness is holding: 66% of coached stores (248 of 378 with follow-up) improved, with a 0.693 lift versus control. The program works.
Looking ahead, 476 stores are scheduled across 64 workshops—277 in the remainder of September and 199 in October. Derron Spencer carries the heaviest October load with 17 workshops and 150 stores. Our OAs are making a difference in the field, and the numbers prove it.

_brief.summary:
Bootcamps are working. Two-thirds of coached stores improved, and the national baseline-to-latest lift of 0.69 points proves the model converts. Danielle Hudson leads YTD with 145 stores coached and a 0.30-point average gain across 420 stores; Dustin Patton's August was the month's most productive at 10 workshops covering 80 stores. Derron Spencer is front-loading the fall with 17 workshops and 150 stores already on the calendar. The pipeline is strong: 64 workshops and 476 stores locked in through October.
August sales broke from the YTD trend. Top-quintile 5-Star stores flipped to positive 1.7% same-store sales growth last month versus negative 0.3% YTD, driven entirely by transactions. The bottom quintile remains the drag, still negative on both sales and traffic. The 5-Star-to-growth correlation holds at 0.11, reinforcing that operational execution translates to the P&L.
Franchisees are moving. Sergio Villasenor delivered a 0.29-point portfolio gain on 270 stores; AKM Shaju pushed 57 net stores from T1 to T3. Our OAs and field operators ran 60 workshops in August, coached 448 stores, and shifted the national average up to 3.36 by June, the year's high mark. That is the field closing the gap, one store at a time.

recognition.name: Danielle Hudson
recognition.why: Danielle delivered the strongest overall swing in the country this period — moving her portfolio from 3.07 to 3.37, a +0.30 average gain that leads all OAs. That pressure showed up in Tier 1, where she cut 37 stores (99 down to 62) and moved 40 stores up to Tier 3. On the coaching side, she ran 5 Boot Camp workshops touching 34 stores this period with 75 stores improving and 109 in follow-up, reflecting a leader who's driving results at scale.

recognition.name: Dustin Patton
recognition.why: Dustin brought the most intensive coaching execution of any OA — 10 Boot Camp workshops reaching 80 stores this period, the highest activity in the group. The impact landed: he cut his Tier 1 count in half (26 down to 13) and pushed 33 stores up to Tier 3, all while starting from an already strong 3.56 base and climbing to 3.77. His Boot Camp lift of 1.422 is the highest in the group by a wide margin, signaling that his coaching is producing real, measurable improvement in the stores he touches.
